title: Episode 48: Build Your Agent: Capstone
description: Designing, writing, testing, and contributing a custom accessibility agent.
concepts: Choosing an agent idea with a real user need
Testing an agent prompt with realistic examples
How the capstone can continue asynchronously after the live event
transcriptText:
﻿[ALEX]
Welcome back. This is the capstone, where everything you've practiced with Git, GitHub, VS Code, Copilot, accessibility, and contribution workflows comes together in one real project.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just, make a toy example and move on.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The expectation is a contribution that could genuinely help a maintainer or user. It might be finished and submitted as a pull request, or it might be a review-ready draft, a contribution plan, an agent file, or another concrete artifact that shows clear purpose, responsibilities, and guardrails.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the choices, what are learners supposed to walk away with?

[ALEX]
A full capstone workflow. You choose a repository, identify a real audience and workflow gap, create or improve an agentic asset, define its boundaries, test it locally or document testing, prepare a pull request or equivalent contribution package, and then either respond to review or explain what review you would seek.

[JAMIE]
And this challenge is the checkpoint, not the whole project.

[ALEX]
Right. The challenge is the evidence. The chapter is the project guide.

[JAMIE]
What counts as an acceptable contribution here?

[ALEX]
Several things. A new agent. An improved agent with better guardrails. A prompt or slash command. Repo-specific custom instructions. A skill or rule reference. A documentation update. Or even an issue triage or scoped proposal for the next agent the project should build.

[JAMIE]
So the common thread is usefulness, not format.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The evidence should show intent, scope, and practical value. For example, an agent file plus testing notes, a diff or pull request link, a prompt file with an example run, a custom instructions file with scope explanation, a skill draft with source notes, or an issue draft that clearly states mission, impact, and guardrails.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What should learners have in place before they start?

[ALEX]
They should already understand fork, branch, commit, push, and pull request workflow. They should have GitHub Copilot or Copilot Free active. They should have explored the Accessibility Agents repository, even if they choose a different capstone path. They should know which repository they want to help and why. And they should be able to explain the impact of their contribution in one or two sentences.

[JAMIE]
That last one matters because if you can't explain the value simply, the scope may still be fuzzy.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[JAMIE]
How long should this take?

[ALEX]
A workshop-ready capstone often takes about sixty to ninety minutes. A polished pull request can take longer, especially if the repo has tests, review rules, or unfamiliar architecture. And it's fully acceptable to finish the workshop with a strong draft and continue asynchronously.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now, there are three main contribution paths.

[JAMIE]
Let me guess. One is the default path, one is a smaller product-focused path, and one is bring your own repository.

[ALEX]
Perfect summary. The paths are Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another repository you care about.

[JAMIE]
How should someone choose well instead of just choosing what sounds interesting?

[ALEX]
Ask five questions. First, impact: who benefits if this merges? Second, fit: does the repository already use agents, prompts, instructions, skills, or automation? Third, scope: can you make a useful change in one small pull request? Fourth, access: can you fork it or at least draft in your own fork? And fifth, safety: can you define guardrails that keep the asset from overreaching?

[JAMIE]
That safety question is easy to overlook when you're excited.

[ALEX]
Yes. A capstone contribution is not stronger because it sounds powerful. It's stronger when its boundaries are clear.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the default route: Accessibility Agents.

[JAMIE]
Why is that the default?

[ALEX]
Because it's built around exactly the kinds of assets you're learning to create: agents, prompts, instructions, skills, and accessibility workflows. It also has a large existing inventory, so learners can study patterns, copy structure, and make a focused contribution without inventing the whole ecosystem from scratch.

[JAMIE]
And the inventory is pretty substantial.

[ALEX]
Yes. The local inventory noted in the source was checked on May thirteenth, twenty twenty-six, and included dozens of agent files, over a hundred prompt files, instruction files, hundreds of skill files, and many top-level GitHub Copilot agents in the dot GitHub agents folder.

[JAMIE]
So if someone wants the most direct path to building a real agent, this is it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's a strong choice if you want clear examples, if you want your work to help accessibility reviewers, developers, document remediators, maintainers, or assistive technology users, and if you want the Challenge 16 autograder path that validates frontmatter, responsibilities, and guardrails.

[JAMIE]
What are good contributions there?

[ALEX]
A small specialist agent for a workflow that is not yet covered. Improving an existing agent's guardrails or output format. Updating stale counts, platform names, or release-note guidance in docs. Adding examples that explain how screen reader users, low-vision users, keyboard-only users, and sighted users should use an agent. Improving prompts so they produce more structured, reviewable output. Or sharpening a skill reference with clearer severity scoring and remediation guidance.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The second route is GLOW.

[JAMIE]
And GLOW is more product-shaped, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. GLOW stands for Guided Layout and Output Workflow. It's a multi-surface accessibility toolkit for auditing, fixing, converting, and generating accessible documents. It spans web, desktop, command-line, VS Code agent tooling, and a Word add-in path.

[JAMIE]
So this is very document accessibility focused.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It centers document accessibility and large-print production. The source specifically notes alignment with the American Council of the Blind Large Print Guidelines, APH submission guidance, Microsoft Accessibility Checker style checks, and WCAG 2.2 AA concepts across formats like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Markdown, PDF, EPUB, HTML, and CSS.

[JAMIE]
That's a lot of surfaces and standards.

[ALEX]
It is, and that's part of why a small, focused contribution can really matter. The source also listed a smaller current inventory than Accessibility Agents, with a handful of agent and prompt files, one instruction file, and one skill file, checked locally on May thirteenth, twenty twenty-six.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of things does GLOW actually do?

[ALEX]
It audits many document formats for accessibility issues. It can auto-fix some Word issues when the fix is deterministic, such as fonts, spacing, emphasis, headings, and margins. It generates ACB-compliant Word templates. It converts among formats using tools like MarkItDown, Pandoc, and LibreOffice. It supports multiple user surfaces. And it works with standards profiles such as ACB 2025 Baseline, APH Submission, and Combined Strict.

[JAMIE]
Why would a learner choose GLOW over Accessibility Agents?

[ALEX]
If they care about documents, large print, Office files, accessible publishing, or user workflows beyond traditional software development. Also if they want a smaller agent surface where one contribution can be very visible, or if they want to connect an agent to a real end-to-end product flow like upload, audit, fix, convert, template, export, and review.

[JAMIE]
What are good GLOW contributions?

[ALEX]
A routing agent that helps users choose between audit, fix, template, export, and convert workflows. Improved instructions for an existing large-print agent with clearer responsibilities and guardrails. A prompt for reviewing release notes against actual current features. Custom instructions that help contributors stay aligned with how GLOW works. Documentation that explains contributor workflows. Or a proposal for rule coverage the product should add next.

[JAMIE]
And there was also a safety note around GLOW.

[ALEX]
Yes, and it's important. In a workflow that touches accessibility remediation, agents should not overclaim certainty, silently modify standards-sensitive content without clear boundaries, or imply legal or compliance guarantees they cannot actually provide. Safer behavior is to explain scope, identify deterministic versus judgment-based fixes, preserve human review, and cite the standards profile or workflow being used.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The third route is another repository.

[JAMIE]
This is the path for learners who already care about a project and want their capstone to land there.

[ALEX]
Exactly. But there are requirements. The repository should have a real audience and a plausible workflow gap. Your planned asset should fit the repo's structure and norms. The contribution should be small enough to review. You need a way to provide evidence even if you cannot merge directly, such as a fork, draft branch, issue proposal, or review-ready document. And you still need responsibilities and guardrails.

[JAMIE]
So even outside the default repositories, the same discipline applies.

[ALEX]
Yes. Good contributions in any repository include project-specific custom instructions, a maintainer-focused agent, issue templates, contribution documentation that is more accessible, prompts for release notes or triage, or a scoped plan for a future agent.

[JAMIE]
In other words, don't force an agent where a prompt, doc update, or instruction file would solve the problem better.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once a learner picks a path, what comes next?

[ALEX]
Define the mission. This is one of the most important steps.

[JAMIE]
Because if the mission is vague, everything downstream gets vague too.

[ALEX]
Correct. A strong mission explains who the asset is for, what workflow it helps with, what it should do, what it should refuse or defer, and what a successful output looks like. Ideally, you can say it in a few plain sentences.

[JAMIE]
Can we make that concrete?

[ALEX]
Sure. Instead of, this agent helps with accessibility, a better mission is, this agent reviews plain-language findings in accessibility audit notes, rewrites them for clarity, preserves technical meaning, and flags places where human reviewers should verify severity or standards references.

[JAMIE]
That already sounds testable.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Mission clarity supports testing, review, and safety.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
After the mission, you write or improve the agentic asset.

[JAMIE]
And the source was intentionally broader than just agent files.

[ALEX]
Yes. The asset might be an agent, prompt, custom instructions file, skill, workflow note, or documentation page. But because this chapter emphasizes agents, it spends special time on agent file structure.

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about location and naming first.

[ALEX]
Agent files should live where the repository expects them. Often that's a dot GitHub agents directory or another established pattern in the project. Naming should be descriptive and consistent, usually with the repo's existing conventions and, for agent files, the expected extension such as dot agent dot md.

[JAMIE]
So don't invent a random folder name or clever title if the repo already has a system.

[ALEX]
Right. Follow the house style.

[JAMIE]
And there was a minimal template idea too.

[ALEX]
Yes. At minimum, an agent asset should make its role obvious. It needs clear frontmatter or metadata expected by the platform, a concise description of responsibilities, explicit guardrails, and usable instructions for how it should respond.

[JAMIE]
The chapter included a named example, the Plain Language Findings Reviewer.

[ALEX]
It did, and that's a very useful model.

[JAMIE]
So what is that example trying to do?

[ALEX]
It's an agent focused on turning findings into plain-language, understandable output without distorting meaning. That means the responsibilities likely include rewriting for clarity, preserving essential technical content, organizing findings so they are reviewable, and helping users understand issues without unnecessary jargon.

[JAMIE]
And just as important, what should it not do?

[ALEX]
It should not invent facts, overstate certainty, claim a legal determination, or silently change the severity or standards basis of a finding without saying so. It should preserve the distinction between what is observed, what is inferred, and what needs human review.

[JAMIE]
That gets us into guardrails.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Guardrails are the boundaries that prevent an agent from becoming misleading or unsafe. They tell the agent when to stay in scope, when to ask for clarification, when to cite uncertainty, when to refuse, and how to present output responsibly.

[JAMIE]
And because this is an accessibility workflow, bad guardrails could create very polished but incorrect guidance.

[ALEX]
Yes, which is why the source emphasizes responsibilities and guardrails as first-class parts of the capstone, not optional polish.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about YAML frontmatter fields?

[ALEX]
The exact fields can vary by environment and tooling, so learners should follow the authoritative docs and the host repository's examples. But the chapter clearly expects valid frontmatter that identifies the agent and supports discoverability and behavior. In practice, that usually means a name or title, a description, and any repository-specific metadata required by the platform or autograder.

[JAMIE]
So the safe rule is: copy the schema used by the target repository, don't improvise.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Especially if the project validates frontmatter automatically.

[JAMIE]
And the learning cards in this part were basically writing advice.

[ALEX]
Yes. Write the asset in plain, testable language. State responsibilities as actions. State guardrails as limits. Prefer specific output expectations over vague aspirations. And design for reviewability, so a maintainer can quickly see what the asset is for and where it might fail.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's move to testing locally.

[JAMIE]
This is the part people skip when they're eager to open the pull request.

[ALEX]
And it's one of the most valuable parts. Testing locally means running realistic prompts or scenarios against the asset before asking others to review it.

[JAMIE]
The source specifically mentions testing with GitHub Copilot Chat.

[ALEX]
Yes. The idea is to load or reference the agent in the environment it is meant for, then try tasks that match its mission. Give it clean cases, messy cases, ambiguous cases, and out-of-scope cases. Observe whether it follows its responsibilities and respects its guardrails.

[JAMIE]
So not just, did it produce words, but did it behave correctly.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A good testing checklist includes whether the asset is discoverable in the expected location, whether frontmatter is valid, whether the mission is understandable, whether outputs are structured and useful, whether the agent avoids overreach, whether it asks for clarification when needed, whether it handles inaccessible or ambiguous input safely, and whether its documentation tells contributors how to use and review it.

[JAMIE]
For blind and low-vision learners, I also want to call out something practical. Structured output is an accessibility issue too.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. If the output is easier to navigate with headings, bullets, short sections, and explicit labels, that helps reviewers using screen readers and everyone else. Accessibility applies to the contribution's behavior and its presentation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once the testing is decent, it's time to open or prepare the pull request.

[ALEX]
Right. Or, if you do not have direct repository access, prepare the equivalent review-ready package.

[JAMIE]
What should that include?

[ALEX]
A clear summary of what you changed and why. The audience or workflow gap you're addressing. Notes about responsibilities and guardrails. Testing notes or examples. Any limitations or open questions. And, if relevant, why you chose an agent versus a prompt, instruction file, or documentation update.

[JAMIE]
So the pull request description is doing teaching work for the maintainer.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A good PR description reduces reviewer effort.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also had a checklist here.

[ALEX]
Yes. Make sure the title is specific. Explain the problem and your solution. Link to any related issues or docs. Describe how you tested. Mention accessibility and safety considerations. Note if the contribution is draft status. And clearly mark anything you want reviewers to focus on.

[JAMIE]
And this is also where Challenge 16 evidence comes in.

[ALEX]
Correct. Evidence can be the pull request itself, the agent file, a documented contribution plan, or a review-ready draft. What matters is that the artifact shows clear purpose, responsibilities, guardrails, and enough substance to evaluate.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
After that comes review.

[JAMIE]
Sometimes the emotional hard part.

[ALEX]
Very true. Responding to review means staying specific, calm, and collaborative. Thank reviewers. Clarify intent when needed. Make small revisions. If you disagree, explain your reasoning with evidence and repository goals in mind. And if you haven't received review yet, describe the kind of review feedback you would actively seek.

[JAMIE]
Like asking, are the guardrails tight enough, is the scope too broad, are the outputs reviewable, does the naming fit the repo, and are the examples realistic?

[ALEX]
Exactly. Mature contributors don't just wait for review. They shape it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How will learners know whether their capstone is strong?

[ALEX]
That's where the rubric helps. The core criteria are usefulness, scope, clarity, responsibilities, guardrails, testing, and review readiness.

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack that a little.

[ALEX]
Useful means it addresses a real need. Scoped means it is small enough to review and realistic for the workshop. Clear means the mission and intended audience are understandable. Responsibilities means the asset's job is explicit. Guardrails means limits and failure boundaries are explicit. Testing means you actually exercised the asset or documented how to do so. Review readiness means a maintainer could meaningfully evaluate it.

[JAMIE]
And what would exceed expectations look like?

[ALEX]
Thoughtful examples. Especially examples that include accessibility-specific user perspectives. Strong documentation. Clean, consistent naming and file placement. Excellent output structure. Clear source notes where standards or guidance matter. Honest discussion of limitations. And a contribution that anticipates reviewer questions before they are asked.

[JAMIE]
So exceeding expectations is not about making the biggest thing.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's about making a well-judged, trustworthy thing.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if someone gets stuck halfway through?

[ALEX]
The chapter gives a universal safety net. Reduce scope, don't abandon the project. If a full agent is too much, contribute a prompt, instructions draft, documentation page, issue proposal, or review-ready plan. If you can't finish testing, document the intended test cases and open questions. If you can't submit upstream, prepare the branch or draft in your fork.

[JAMIE]
So there is always a valid next smaller step.

[ALEX]
Yes. And that's an important professional habit. When blocked, produce the clearest useful artifact you can.

[JAMIE]
That is reassuring.

[ALEX]
It should be. The goal is not perfection on demand. The goal is a credible, helpful contribution process.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap, I want to make sure we include the administrative and source guidance too.

[ALEX]
Good call. The chapter points learners to related appendices for agents, Copilot, and Markdown reference material. It also names authoritative sources, especially VS Code documentation on custom agents and the agents window, plus GitHub documentation on Copilot agents and customization support.

[JAMIE]
And there was a section-level source map idea.

[ALEX]
Right. That's a reminder to ground your contribution in official documentation and the repository's current patterns, especially because agent tooling evolves quickly. If there's any mismatch between an older example and current platform behavior, the authoritative docs and the target repository's present implementation should win.

[JAMIE]
That's particularly important for frontmatter schemas, support matrices, and where custom instructions or agents are actually supported.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
So if you're about to start, here is the practical sequence. Pick a repository. State the audience and workflow gap. Choose the smallest useful asset. Define responsibilities and guardrails. Put the file in the right place with the right naming and metadata. Test realistic scenarios in Copilot Chat or the repo's expected environment. Prepare a clear pull request or review-ready package. Then respond thoughtfully to feedback.

[JAMIE]
And if you're unsure which path to take, Accessibility Agents is the strongest default, GLOW is excellent for document and large-print workflows, and another repository is great if you already understand the users and the problem.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Make it real, make it scoped, make it safe, and make it reviewable.

[JAMIE]
That's the capstone.

[ALEX]
It is. And if you produce something a maintainer could genuinely use, even as a draft, you've done the work this lesson is aiming for.

# Capstone Project: Contribute an Impactful Agent

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix L: Agents Reference](appendix-l-agents-reference.md) | [Appendix K: Copilot Reference](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md) | [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [VS Code Docs: Custom agents](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/custom-agents) | [VS Code Docs: Agents window](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/agents/agents-window) | [GitHub Docs: About GitHub Copilot agents](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/using-extensions-to-integrate-external-tools-with-copilot-chat)

> **Day 2, Block 4 Material (Capstone)**
>
> Everything you have learned comes together here. You will choose a real repository, design or improve an agentic contribution, test it, and prepare a pull request or contribution plan that would help that project. Accessibility Agents is still a strong default path, but it is not the only valid path.

## Table of Contents

1. [The Capstone Project](#1-the-capstone-project)
2. [Choose Your Contribution Path](#2-choose-your-contribution-path)
3. [Project Option: Accessibility Agents](#3-project-option-accessibility-agents)
4. [Project Option: GLOW](#4-project-option-glow)
5. [Project Option: Another Repository](#5-project-option-another-repository)
6. [Define Your Mission](#6-define-your-mission)
7. [Write or Improve the Agentic Asset](#7-write-or-improve-the-agentic-asset)
8. [Test Locally](#8-test-locally)
9. [Open or Prepare Your Pull Request](#9-open-or-prepare-your-pull-request)
10. [Respond to Review](#10-respond-to-review)
11. [Capstone Rubric](#11-capstone-rubric)
12. [If You Get Stuck](#12-if-you-get-stuck)

---

> **Challenge 16: Capstone Project.** This is the culminating challenge of the workshop. Your evidence can be a pull request, an agent file, a documented contribution plan, or a review-ready draft that shows clear purpose, responsibilities, and guardrails.

## 1. The Capstone Project

The capstone is bigger than one challenge and bigger than one repository. Challenge 16 is the checkpoint where you show evidence. The chapter is the project guide.

You will:

1. Choose a repository where an agentic contribution would be useful.
2. Identify a real audience and a real workflow gap.
3. Create or improve an agent, prompt, custom instruction, skill, workflow, or documentation page that helps that repository.
4. Define clear responsibilities and guardrails.
5. Test the contribution locally or document how it should be tested.
6. Open a pull request, prepare a review-ready branch, or write a contribution plan when you do not have repository access.
7. Respond to review or describe what review feedback you would seek.

This is not a simulation. Your work should be useful to a real maintainer, even if it remains a draft during the workshop.

### What Counts as a Capstone Contribution

The following table lists valid capstone contribution types.

| Contribution Type | Example | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New agent | A GLOW agent that audits uploaded-document error messages for plain language | Agent file plus testing notes |
| Improved agent | Better guardrails for an Accessibility Agents reviewer agent | Diff or PR link plus explanation |
| Prompt or slash command | A prompt that guides maintainers through release-note updates | Prompt file plus example run |
| Custom instructions | Repo-specific instructions that prevent inaccessible UI patterns | Instructions file plus scope explanation |
| Skill or rule reference | A reusable rule pack for large-print document checks | Skill draft plus source notes |
| Documentation update | A contribution guide that explains how to add agents safely | PR link or review-ready draft |
| Issue triage plan | A scoped proposal for an agent the project should build next | Issue draft with mission, impact, and guardrails |

### What You Need Before Starting

- [ ] You understand the fork, branch, commit, push, and PR workflow from [Chapter 18](18-fork-and-contribute.md).
- [ ] You have GitHub Copilot or Copilot Free active from [Chapter 16](16-github-copilot.md).
- [ ] You have explored Accessibility Agents in [Chapter 19](19-accessibility-agents.md), even if you choose a different capstone repository.
- [ ] You know which repository you want to help and why.
- [ ] You can explain the impact of your contribution in one or two sentences.

### Time Estimate

Most students complete a workshop-ready capstone in 60 to 90 minutes. A polished pull request can take longer, especially when the target project has tests, review requirements, or unfamiliar architecture. It is acceptable to finish the workshop with a clear draft and continue asynchronously.

---

## 2. Choose Your Contribution Path

Freedom is encouraged. Choose a repository where your work can be genuinely useful.

The following table compares the recommended paths.

| Path | Best For | Good Contribution Ideas |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accessibility Agents | Learners who want the most direct agent-building path | Add a focused agent, improve guardrails, update docs, refine prompts, improve skills |
| GLOW | Learners interested in document accessibility, large print, Office files, web apps, desktop apps, or user workflows | Add a GLOW-focused agent, improve `.github` customizations, document contributor workflows, propose rule coverage |
| Another repository | Learners with a project they already care about | Add project-specific custom instructions, an agent for maintainer workflows, accessible contribution docs, or issue templates |

### Choosing Well

Ask these questions before you choose:

- **Impact:** Who would benefit if this contribution were merged?
- **Fit:** Does the repository already use agents, prompts, instructions, skills, or automation?
- **Scope:** Can you make a useful change in one small pull request?
- **Access:** Can you fork the repository or create a draft in your own fork?
- **Safety:** Can you define guardrails that prevent the agent from overreaching?

---

## 3. Project Option: Accessibility Agents

[Accessibility Agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents) is the default capstone path because it is built around agents, prompts, instructions, skills, and accessibility workflows.

Current local inventory checked May 13, 2026:

| Asset Type | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Agent files (`*.agent.md`) | 83 |
| Prompt files (`*.prompt.md`) | 132 |
| Instruction files (`*.instructions.md`) | 10 |
| Skill files (`SKILL.md`) | 207 |
| Top-level GitHub Copilot agents in `.github/agents/` | 80 |

### Why Choose Accessibility Agents

- You want to build or improve an actual agent.
- You want clear examples to copy and adapt.
- You want your contribution to help accessibility reviewers, developers, document remediators, GitHub maintainers, or assistive technology users.
- You want the Challenge 16 autograder path that validates agent frontmatter, responsibilities, and guardrails.

### Good Accessibility Agents Contributions

- Add a small specialist agent for an uncovered accessibility workflow.
- Improve an existing agent's guardrails or output format.
- Update stale counts, platform names, or release-note guidance in documentation.
- Add examples that show how screen reader, low vision, keyboard-only, and sighted users should use an agent.
- Improve prompt files so they produce more structured, reviewable output.
- Improve a skill reference with clearer severity scoring or remediation guidance.

---

## 4. Project Option: GLOW

[GLOW](https://github.com/Community-Access/glow) stands for **Guided Layout & Output Workflow**. It is a multi-surface accessibility toolkit for auditing, fixing, converting, and generating accessible documents. It includes a web app, desktop tooling, a CLI-oriented workflow, a VS Code agent toolkit, and a Word add-in path.

GLOW focuses on document accessibility and large-print production. It enforces the American Council of the Blind Large Print Guidelines, APH submission guidance, Microsoft Accessibility Checker-style checks, and WCAG 2.2 AA concepts across formats such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Markdown, PDF, EPUB, HTML, and CSS.

Current local inventory checked May 13, 2026:

| Asset Type | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Agent files (`*.agent.md`) | 5 |
| Prompt files (`*.prompt.md`) | 5 |
| Instruction files (`*.instructions.md`) | 1 |
| Skill files (`SKILL.md`) | 1 |

### What GLOW Does

- Audits Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Markdown, PDF, EPUB, HTML, and CSS for accessibility issues.
- Auto-fixes Word document issues where the change is deterministic, such as fonts, spacing, emphasis, headings, and margins.
- Generates ACB-compliant Word templates.
- Converts documents to Markdown, accessible HTML, Word, EPUB 3, PDF, and DAISY-oriented outputs through MarkItDown, Pandoc, LibreOffice, and related tooling.
- Provides web, desktop, CLI, VS Code, and Word add-in surfaces.
- Supports standards profiles such as ACB 2025 Baseline, APH Submission, and Combined Strict.

### Why Choose GLOW

- You care about documents, large print, Office files, or accessible publishing.
- You want a smaller agent surface where one contribution can make a visible difference.
- You want to connect agents to a real product workflow: upload, audit, fix, convert, template, export, review.
- You want to help users who may not think of themselves as developers.

### Good GLOW Contributions

- Add a GLOW agent that helps users choose between Audit, Fix, Template, Export, and Convert workflows.
- Improve the existing large-print agent instructions with clearer responsibilities and guardrails.
- Add a prompt for reviewing release notes against current GLOW features.
- Add custom instructions for web UI accessibility, plain-language findings, or large-print documentation consistency.
- Write documentation that explains how contributors should test document accessibility changes.
- Draft an issue for a future agent, such as a plain-language findings reviewer, batch-audit triage assistant, or Word add-in accessibility reviewer.

### GLOW Safety Notes

- GLOW handles documents that may contain personal, educational, medical, or organizational information. Do not put private user documents into public prompts or issues.
- Auto-fix workflows must be conservative. An agent should explain proposed fixes and preserve author intent.
- Large-print rules can affect pagination and layout. Document tradeoffs instead of pretending every fix is neutral.
- When a rule comes from ACB, APH, Microsoft Accessibility Checker, or WCAG, cite the source or name the profile.

---

## 5. Project Option: Another Repository

You may choose another repository if the contribution is meaningful and reviewable. This can be your own project, a classmate's project, a community repository, or another open source project you care about.

### Requirements for Another Repository

- The work must help the repository, not just satisfy the workshop.
- The contribution must have a clear audience.
- The contribution must be small enough to review.
- The contribution must include responsibilities and guardrails when it involves an agent or automated workflow.
- If you cannot open a pull request, write a review-ready issue or contribution plan instead.

### Good Contributions in Any Repository

- Add `.github/copilot-instructions.md` that teaches Copilot the project's accessibility and contribution standards.
- Add a custom agent for triaging issues, reviewing docs, checking release notes, or auditing accessibility.
- Add a prompt file for a repeated maintainer task.
- Improve issue templates or PR templates so contributors provide better accessibility context.
- Write contributor documentation that explains how to test with keyboard, screen reader, and high contrast workflows.

---

## 6. Define Your Mission

A good capstone mission solves a specific, recurring problem. It does not try to do everything.

Write a one-sentence mission statement before editing files:

> "My contribution helps [who] by [doing what] when [in what situation]."

Examples:

- "My agent helps GLOW contributors by checking whether release notes describe user-facing document accessibility changes clearly."
- "My prompt helps Accessibility Agents maintainers by turning a release note into repo documentation updates with screen reader, low vision, and sighted guidance."
- "My custom instructions help my project avoid inaccessible React patterns when Copilot generates forms and dialogs."

Post this mission statement in your Challenge 16 issue comment so a buddy or facilitator can give early feedback.

---

## 7. Write or Improve the Agentic Asset

Your asset may be an agent file, prompt file, instruction file, skill, or documentation update. If you are writing an agent, use the structure below.

### Agent File Location and Naming

Follow the target repository's conventions. Common locations include:

```text
.github/agents/your-agent-name.agent.md
agents/your-agent-name.agent.md
community-agents/your-agent-name.agent.md
```

Use lowercase with hyphens. Example: `.github/agents/plain-language-findings.agent.md`.

### Minimal Agent File Template

```markdown
---
name: "Plain Language Findings Reviewer"
description: "Reviews accessibility audit findings for plain language, actionable remediation, and user impact."
---

# Plain Language Findings Reviewer

You are an accessibility documentation specialist focused on making audit findings clear, actionable, and respectful.

## Responsibilities

- Review finding text for plain language and specific remediation steps
- Identify vague phrases that do not explain user impact
- Check that findings name the affected workflow or assistive technology when known
- Suggest revised wording without changing the technical meaning

## Guardrails

- Never claim a finding is fixed unless the user provides verification evidence
- Do not remove severity or WCAG references
- If the technical meaning is unclear, ask for clarification instead of guessing
- Preserve project terminology unless it is inaccurate or inaccessible
```

### YAML Frontmatter Fields

The following table describes the common agent frontmatter fields.

| Field | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | Yes | Display name for the agent |
| `description` | Yes | One-sentence description of what the agent does and when it should be used |
| `tools` | Project-specific | Tool list when the target platform requires explicit tools |

### Learning Cards: Writing the Asset

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Use the Command Palette to create or open files, then save the asset in the target repository's expected folder.
- Use `Ctrl+Shift+O` to move by heading and confirm that Responsibilities and Guardrails are easy to find.
- Use `Alt+F2` for long Copilot responses while testing the agent.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Keep frontmatter fields on separate lines and use a consistent heading hierarchy.
- Use Markdown Preview to verify that headings, lists, and examples are visually clear.
- Avoid long single-line bullets that require horizontal scrolling at high zoom.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Use the Outline view to scan the structure before testing.
- Compare your file with two existing examples in the target repository.
- Check that the file name, `name`, and description all point to the same focused mission.

</details>

---

## 8. Test Locally

Before opening a pull request, test or review your work.

### Testing With GitHub Copilot Chat

1. Open VS Code with the target repository.
2. Save your agent, prompt, instruction, or documentation file.
3. Open GitHub Copilot Chat (`Ctrl+Alt+I`) or run **Chat: Open Chat** from the Command Palette.
4. Invoke the agent or prompt if supported. Example: `@plain-language-findings review this audit finding for clarity`.
5. Observe whether the output follows the responsibilities and guardrails.
6. Revise the asset and test again.

### Testing Checklist

- [ ] The contribution has a clear mission.
- [ ] Responsibilities are specific and action-oriented.
- [ ] Guardrails prevent overreach.
- [ ] Output is useful, specific, and accessible.
- [ ] The contribution follows the target repository's naming and folder conventions.
- [ ] You documented any limitations or future work.

---

## 9. Open or Prepare Your Pull Request

### Tool Cards: Open Your Capstone PR

**VS Code Desktop:**

1. Push your branch: `Ctrl+Shift+P` then **Git: Push**.
2. Run **GitHub Pull Requests: Create Pull Request** from the Command Palette.
3. Set the base repository to the project you chose.
4. Fill in the title and description.

**GitHub.com:**

1. Navigate to your fork on GitHub.
2. Activate **Contribute** then **Open pull request**.
3. Verify the base repository and compare branch.
4. Create the pull request.

**GitHub CLI:**

```bash
git push -u origin your-branch
gh pr create --repo OWNER/REPOSITORY
```

### PR Description Checklist

- [ ] Mission statement
- [ ] Repository path chosen: Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another project
- [ ] What changed
- [ ] Why it matters
- [ ] How you tested it
- [ ] Known limitations or follow-up ideas
- [ ] Accessibility impact

### Challenge 16 Evidence

Post one of these in your Challenge 16 issue:

- A pull request link
- A branch link with the changed file
- A draft agent file pasted or linked
- A contribution plan with mission, responsibilities, guardrails, and target repository
- A review of a peer's capstone PR or a peer-simulation PR

If you use the Accessibility Agents autograder path, it checks agent file structure in `agents/` or `community-agents/`: frontmatter, responsibilities, and guardrails. If you choose GLOW or another project, your facilitator reviews the evidence against the same principles.

---

## 10. Respond to Review

After you submit or share your capstone, a buddy, facilitator, or maintainer may review it.

Reviewers look for:

- **Clarity:** Can someone understand the contribution in 10 seconds?
- **Specificity:** Are responsibilities concrete and actionable?
- **Safety:** Do guardrails prevent harmful or overconfident behavior?
- **Usefulness:** Would this help a real user or maintainer?
- **Fit:** Does it follow the target repository's conventions?

Respond to review one comment at a time. If a reviewer asks for a change, make the edit, commit, push, and reply with what changed.

---

## 11. Capstone Rubric

The capstone is assessed as a real contribution, not just as a file format exercise.

### Core Criteria

The following table lists the capstone evaluation criteria.

| Criterion | Meets Expectations |
| --- | --- |
| Repository choice | The learner can explain why the chosen repository benefits from the contribution |
| Mission clarity | The contribution has a focused mission statement |
| Responsibilities | The agentic asset names concrete actions it should perform |
| Guardrails | The contribution includes boundaries, limitations, or safety notes |
| Accessibility impact | The work accounts for screen reader, low vision, keyboard-only, cognitive, or document accessibility needs when relevant |
| Evidence | The learner provides a PR, draft, branch, issue, or contribution plan |
| Review readiness | The contribution is small enough for someone else to review |

### What Exceeds Expectations Looks Like

- The contribution includes examples of expected input and output.
- The PR description explains tradeoffs and limitations.
- The learner tests with Copilot Chat or the VS Code Agents window and documents the result.
- The learner responds thoughtfully to review feedback.
- The contribution improves existing documentation, counts, or setup instructions alongside the agentic asset.

---

## 12. If You Get Stuck

The following table lists common capstone blockers and recovery steps.

| Problem | What To Do |
| --- | --- |
| I cannot choose a repository | Choose Accessibility Agents if you want the clearest agent path, or GLOW if you want document accessibility and large-print impact |
| I cannot think of an idea | Find one repeated maintainer task and write an agent or prompt for that task |
| I do not have permission to open a PR | Create a draft in your fork or write a contribution issue with mission, responsibilities, and guardrails |
| The repository has no agents yet | Add repo-level custom instructions or propose the first agent in a draft issue |
| My agent does too much | Split the mission until it fits one sentence |
| Copilot ignores the guardrails | Make the guardrails more explicit and test with the same prompt again |
| The external project has different conventions | Follow that project's README and CONTRIBUTING file first, then explain any uncertainty in your PR |
| I finished but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 16 reference solution](solutions/solution-16-capstone.md), then ask for review |

### The Universal Safety Net

If everything else fails, post this on your Challenge 16 issue:

> I attempted the capstone project and here is what happened:
>
> **Repository I chose:** [repository]
> **What I tried:** [specific actions]
> **What I expected:** [what should have happened]
> **What actually happened:** [error or unexpected result]
> **What I learned:** [even from failure, what do I understand now?]

This is always useful evidence. A learner who explains a failure thoughtfully has learned more than one who followed the happy path without thinking.

voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
